Fasolia Green Bean Stew

Tunisian · Easy · Serves 4

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
Fasolia — green beans simmered slow in tomato and garlic until the beans go olive-silk and the sauce runs thick enough to hold them — is the region's summer-market pot: the Maghreb's answer to the whole Mediterranean's braised-bean argument, run with the #91 harissa's warmth or the chile's quieter whisper. The beans' long cooking is the point — this is not a crisp bean's dish — and the pot's leftover, next day, is the dish's better half.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

Ingredients

  • or over rice, or with the #9 ta'ameya's fried eggs
- **Cook the beans past crisp — far past.** The fasolia's beans surrender: 35 to 40 minutes at the simmer, until olive-green and silk-tender, their flavor concentrated and their texture yielding. The al dente instinct is the dish's enemy; this is the braised bean's own clock. - **The bridge:** none needed — the whole pot is the daily row. The harissa-or-flakes choice is the house's fire register; the beans carry either.

Fasolia Green Bean Stew

Prep: 20 minutes · Cook: 45 minutes · Total: About 1 hour 5 minutes · Serves 4

Ingredients

Ingredients

  • 600 g green beans, topped, tailed, snapped in half (about 550 g trimmed)
  • 3 tbsp olive oil (about 40 g); 1 onion (about 150 g), sliced
  • 5 cloves garlic (about 20 g), sliced; 1 tbsp tomato paste (about 15 g)
  • 500 g tomatoes, grated, or 1 large can crushed; 1 tsp cumin; 1 tsp paprika; ½ tsp chile flakes or 1 tsp harissa (#91)
  • 1 tsp salt; 100 ml water (about 100 g); a fist of cilantro (about 15 g), half tied in the pot, half at the finish
  • Optional: 150 g potatoes, wedged (the heartier school), or a whole chile pricked
  • To serve: bread (about 250 g), lemon, the #116 cumin salt — or over rice, or with the #9 ta'ameya's fried eggs

Instructions

  1. **The base (8 minutes).** Warm the oil; soften the onion 5 minutes; add the garlic, the tomato paste, and the spices, frying 1–2 minutes to the pot's perfume and the paste's darkened edge. Checkpoint — the paste's raw note cooked out, the fragrance warm — the same small fried base the #43 loubia runs, the region's shared pot-beginning.
  2. **The long simmer (40 minutes).** The tomatoes, the water, the beans, the salt, and the tied herbs — bring to a bare simmer, cover ajar, and cook 35–40 minutes, stirring twice, until the beans are olive-silk and the sauce has thickened to coat them heavily. The potatoes (if running) in at the 25-minute mark. Checkpoint — the sauce's end: thick, tomato-dark, clinging — the beans visible through the coat but barely. A bean's bite: yielding entirely, its flavor deep and sweet — the long cook's work. If the sauce runs thin, uncover the last 10 minutes and reduce.
  3. **The finish and the service.** Off the flame: the fresh cilantro, a thread of raw olive oil, the lemon at the table — served with bread, over rice, or beside the fried eggs of the fuller table. Checkpoint — eating test: the beans' olive silk in the tomato's thick coat — garlic and cumin running through, the harissa's warmth behind — the raw oil's green and the lemon's lift at the swallow, the bread sopping. Next day, from the refrigerator's pot, the beans steeped overnight — the sauce darker, the flavor deeper — the fasolia's own second answer.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Beans still squeak at the biteUnder-simmeredThe 35–40 minute surrender
Sauce thin, poolsTomatoes watery or under-reducedThe uncovered last 10
Pot flat despite the baseGarlic or herbs shyBoth carry \u2014 the garlic leads

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- Keeps 4 days refrigerated, improving daily; the reheat is a gentle covered simmer. Freezes 2 months. The #43 loubia is the white bean's own pot; this record is the green bean's. - Variations: the potato-hearted winter school, the egg-nested table version. The #100 matbucha is this pot's cooked-salad cousin.

methodSteps.chefsNote: the braised green bean runs the whole Mediterranean's summer kitchens — the French niçoise's far cousins, the Italian fagiolini al pomodoro, the Greek fasolakia — and the Maghreb's distinction is the harissa-or-chile's warm register and the cumin's earth beneath the tomato. The doctrine all these kitchens share: the bean's surrender is the dish — and the pot's next-day is the argument's proof, the flavors married overnight. Cook the pot for the second day and eat the first honestly.
